name: Patriot (American Revolution)
scope: The political ideas of the American Patriots (also called Whigs, Revolutionaries, Continentals or Rebels), the colonists of 1763-1783 who resisted British rule and built the case for independence. The defining sources present it as a Whig/republican outlook: rights as Englishmen under the British constitution, no taxation without representation, the corrupting power of a standing army and a distant crown, civic virtue and equality, then the natural-rights and popular-sovereignty language of the Declaration of Independence and Paine's Common Sense. Strands: radical Patriots (the Adamses, Paine) against moderates; after the war Patriots divided between devotees of republican order (Washington, Madison, John Adams, Hamilton, Jay) and democratic impulses (Henry, Franklin, Jefferson). Texts by Loyalists written against the Patriots are critics. Excludes the Loyalists, the later Federalist and Jeffersonian parties and the Patriot movement of the modern American right.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Articles of Confederation bar Congress from granting any title of nobility, and Common Sense attacks hereditary succession and the distinction of rank it rests on.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: The Declaration lists the quartering of troops, a standing army and foreign mercenaries among its grievances, calls Britain's jurisdiction foreign to the colonial constitution, and the Patriots resisted by arms.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Declaration of Independence, as the American Yawp quotes it, holds that governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed"; the Stamp Act resistance likewise rested on taxation only by consent.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: The Declaration lists the denial of the benefits of trial by jury among its grievances.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Common Sense attacks hereditary succession as against the equal rights of nature and scripture.

elective-rulers.rationale: Common Sense rejects hereditary monarchy and proposes that the continent's president be chosen by Congress.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The Declaration also gives the people as a body the right to alter or abolish their government.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Common Sense rejects monarchy and hereditary succession, and the Declaration calls the king a tyrant unfit to rule a free people.

people-in-arms.rationale: Marina (section on militia versus standing army) says radical Whiggism leaned toward a people's militia against the crown's standing army, while less radical members of the revolutionary coalition thought along conventional lines of an organized army.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: The Declaration derives just powers from the consent of the governed, not from personal bonds to a ruler.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: The Declaration holds it the people's right and duty to throw off a government that works a long train of abuses, which the Patriots did by war.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The Declaration charges the king with obstructing the naturalisation of foreigners and refusing to encourage their migration to the colonies.

resist-oppression-despite-death.rationale: The Declaration calls it the people's duty, not merely right, to throw off despotism, and its signers pledge their lives, fortunes and sacred honor.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: The Declaration holds that when a government becomes destructive of rights "it is the Right of the People to alter or to abolish it" (American Yawp), and Britannica describes the Revolution as the insurrection through which the colonies threw off British rule.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Common Sense mocks the title of sacred majesty for a king, saying his exaltation cannot be justified on equal natural rights or on scripture.

term-limits.rationale: The Articles of Confederation bar any person from being a delegate to Congress for more than three years in any six.

universal-morality.rationale: The Declaration holds its truths about equality, unalienable rights and government by consent self-evident for all men and refers to the laws of nature and of nature's God.

summary: The American Patriots, also called Whigs or Revolutionaries, were the colonists of 1763-1783 who resisted British rule. Their outlook combined the rights of Englishmen, no taxation without consent and a radical-Whig fear of standing armies with the Declaration of Independence's claims that government rests on the consent of the governed and that the people may alter or abolish a destructive one. Radical Patriots leaned toward a people's militia while moderates favoured a conventional army.
